accountable.title: Simbolik: Security Toolkit for Solidity
snippets: None of the raised funds is used for closed-source development or operations.

All work funded by this round ships under BSD-3 to our public GitHub repository.


Roadmap


The five deliverables below ship *consecutively, in priority order*, as funding accumulates.
Anything funded ships in full; anything underfunded does not start.

Budgets cover engineering, documentation, and release operations.


1.

Kontrol formal verification, integrated — $0 - $15,000


Kontrol (Runtime Verification’s Foundry-native formal verification engine) becomes a built-in Simbolik feature.

Stack-too-deep detector with auto-fix — $15,000 - $25,000


Stack-too-deep is one of Solidity’s oldest and most-criticized rough edges; the annual Solidity developer surveys have repeatedly ranked it among the language’s top compiler frustrations.

AI-assisted, coverage-guided test synthesis — $25,000 - $40,000


Simbolik gains a test-synthesis feature that uses an LLM to generate Foundry tests, informed by its existing test coverage reports.

Web-hosted Simbolik for browser-based source review — $40,000-$55,000


A hosted, browser-based Simbolik makes any on-chain-verified contract or transaction auditable directly from a URL, with sources resolved via Sourcify and no local installation required.


Two entry points are supported: by contract address (`simbolik.dev/contract/<chain>/<address>`) and by transaction hash (`simbolik.dev/tx/<chain>/<tx-hash>`).

Interactive symbolic execution — $55,000+


Kontrol already exposes the full internal state of a proof, but only through a terminal UI and only at the level of raw KEVM configurations — word stacks, memory regions, 256-bit storage keys, path conditions over symbolic words.

For developers fluent in Solidity, that is a steep barrier between writing a specification and understanding why it does or does not go through.


This milestone closes the gap on two axes: the TUI is replaced by a graphical interface in the Simbolik test explorer, with breakpoints, single-step and step-over controls, and call-stack navigation; and every paused state is lifted from KEVM back to its Solidity meaning — storage slots as their declared mappings and arrays, packed bytes as struct fields, the symbolic word stack as named locals, path conditions as predicates over Solidity expressions.

The engineer reasoning about a proof sees the contract they wrote, not the bytecode it compiled to.


This milestone is also where any excess funding lands.

Because the final round size is unknown, we are not committing to a specific scope here: every dollar above $55,000 goes toward this deliverable, in priority order — graphical interface first, then progressively wider Solidity-level state lifting.

snippets:
And the protocols that hold their funds have every incentive to downplay the risks rather than surface them.

That gap is what TID Research exists to close.

What we do

At TID Research (Today in DeFi), we publish independent risk ratings for DeFi assets and protocols on Ethereum and its L2s.

Our goal is simple: give users the diligence layer they need to protect themselves before the next exploit hits, not after.

Our existing reports are live at https://tidresearch.com/reports, alongside dashboards at https://tidresearch.com/dashboards/ that let users monitor exposures across the protocols they actually use.

For assets, our risk reports systematically cover:

  • Smart contract risk — audit history, code maturity, upgradeability patterns, and the actual surface area an attacker would target.

But there's another layer of security that determines whether ordinary users actually keep their money: the layer of information asymmetry between protocols and the people using them.

A user can hold an asset that's economically broken without knowing it.

Every one of those scenarios ends in the same place: users lose funds, trust in Ethereum erodes, and the ecosystem absorbs another reputational hit.

Independent, rigorous, free-to-read risk research is public goods user protection infrastructure.

And it's exactly the kind of work that markets systematically underfund, because the people who need it most can't afford to pay for it, and the protocols being analyzed have an interest in not paying for it.

That's why this round exists, and why we're applying.

Why us

TID Research has been operating in DeFi research and farming for years.

The vast majority of what we produce is public goods — distributed widely so that the maximum number of users benefit, not gated behind paywalls only institutions can afford.

What funding will support

A grant from this round will directly fund expansion of our independent security and risk research:

  1. More asset risk reports, covering a wider range of LSTs, LRTs, stablecoins, yield-bearing tokens, and structured products on Ethereum mainnet and major L2s (Arbitrum, Base, Optimism, Hyperliquid, etc.).
  2. Protocol-level risk reports, going deeper than asset coverage into the lending markets, DEXes, perps platforms, and structured product venues where most user funds actually sit.
  3. Faster post-incident analysis — when the next exploit happens, we want to publish technical breakdowns within hours, not days, so users on related protocols can act before contagion spreads.
  4. Improved dashboards and monitoring, so users can track the risk profile of their actual on-chain positions in real time, not just read static reports.
  5. Open methodology — funding lets us document and open-source our risk frameworks so other researchers, DAOs, and risk teams can build on top of them.

Conflicts and transparency

We take editorial independence seriously.

Funding from this round will be deployed exclusively toward independent research outputs published as public goods.

The ask

If you've ever lost money to a DeFi exploit, or watched a friend lose money, or held an asset that broke and wished someone had warned you sooner — that's the gap we're trying to close.

accountable.title: AgnopraxLab
snippets:
These “in-between” gaps are exactly where dangerous issues can remain unnoticed.

If the network is not safe, the protocol is not truly safe.


What We Want To Do

We want to build a new security testing framework that looks at Ethereum’s network communication in a more complete and realistic way.

Instead of checking isolated pieces one by one, our approach will simulate how a peer behaves over time:

  • how it joins the network
  • how it exchanges messages
  • how it reacts to changing conditions
  • how different communication layers affect each other

This helps us find problems that traditional tools are likely to miss.


Why This Is Important

Our goal is simple:

Find hidden weaknesses earlier

Before attackers or real-world failures expose them.

Test the system more like the real world

Because real networks are dynamic, messy, and full of interactions—not neat isolated steps.

Protect the broader Ethereum ecosystem

A stronger network layer benefits:

  • client teams
  • node operators
  • developers
  • users
  • the long-term reliability of Ethereum itself


What This Project Will Deliver

Open-Source Security Tooling

We will release an open-source toolkit that others can use, extend, and integrate into their own testing workflows.

Practical Security Improvements

We will work with client teams to help turn findings into real fixes, patches, and improvements.

Public Knowledge for the Ecosystem

The project will also produce:

  • research publications
  • vulnerability advisories
  • public writeups that help the wider community learn and improve


What Makes This Project Different

Most existing efforts check only limited parts of the network.

Our project focuses on the whole communication journey, not just isolated moments.

That means we are not only asking:

“Can this single message break something?”

We are also asking:

“What happens when many steps unfold together over time, the way they do in the real network?”

That broader perspective is where many important security problems can be discovered.


Early Proof That This Works

We are not starting from zero.

Our earlier work already produced:

  • a working security-testing prototype
  • real bug discoveries in major Ethereum clients
  • direct engagement with development teams
  • a strong engineering foundation for this next step

This gives us confidence that the new project can create practical value for the ecosystem.


Codebase

  • GitHub Repository: AgnopraxLab / D2PFuzz

Selected Bugs We Found


  • go-ethereum issue #31471
  • reth issue #15255
  • erigon issue #13931
  • besu issue #8445
  • besu issue #8339


What We Will Do With Funding

Our current work has built a strong foundation in testing Ethereum’s network layer — the part of the system that allows nodes to communicate, exchange messages, and stay connected.

With funding, we want to take the next step: moving from testing how Ethereum nodes talk to testing how they agree.

This is important because Ethereum’s security does not depend on communication alone.

Compared with network message fuzzing, consensus fuzzing is more demanding because it must reason about:

  • how protocol state evolves over time
  • how different clients handle the same sequence of events
  • how edge cases affect agreement, finality, and fork choice
  • how unexpected inputs or timing conditions may expose hidden implementation differences

The funding will be used primarily for two core needs:

  • Engineer salaries
  • To support the research, development, implementation, testing, and maintenance required to extend the framework from network-layer fuzzing to consensus-focused fuzzing.
  • Server rental and computing infrastructure
  • To run large-scale fuzzing campaigns, long-duration experiments, multi-client validation, regression testing, and continuous security testing workflows.

accountable.title: Symproof by BlockScience & Shield3
snippets: It codifies both our longstanding open-source and proprietary work in the underlying math and security logic that has protected billions in TVL and refined grant programs by flagging and reducing fraud.

What It Is Not


What Symproof Is

  • A Pythonic framework built on SymPy for making the mathematical assumptions of DeFi and ZK protocols explicit, hashed, and independently verifiable
  • A design-phase tool - it operates before Solidity is written, on the formulas themselves
  • A growing library of reusable, pre-proved components for common Ethereum formula patterns: AMM arithmetic, ZK circuits, fixed-point rounding, vault invariants
  • Accessible to security engineers who are not specialists in symbolic mathematics - the repo ships with structured LLM guidance that assists in writing correct proofs
  • Equipped with falsity and consistency guards - seal() rejects self-contradictory axiom sets and proofs that depend on undeclared load-bearing assumptions, before verification runs


What Symproof Is Not

  • A replacement for Certora, Halmos, or Slither - it sits beneath them, ensuring the specification those tools verify is itself sound
  • A Solidity verifier or runtime monitor
  • A full theorem prover - it is less rigorous than Lean or Coq, more rigorous than auditor inspection, and designed for the workflow of practicing security engineers


In short: Symproof tells you what properties to prove and verifies the math behind them - formal verification then checks that the code delivers those properties, and fuzzing finds edge cases at runtime.

The three phases follow a deliberate dependency order.


Phase 1 is a prerequisite for everything else.

The provenance infrastructure (citation tracking, inherited axiom marking, foundation enforcement) is stabilized here as the documented backbone that all domain libraries build on.


Phase 2 establishes credibility and accessibility through application.

This is the reference case that makes Phase 3 libraries trustworthy rather than theoretical.


Phase 3 is where the compounding effect begins.

The value accumulates across every subsequent audit that uses the same formula patterns, where audit by audit, the baseline rises.


The extent of Phase 3 scales with available funding.
The priority order is listed in the Use of Funds section.

The measure of success is not components shipped but whether a practicing Ethereum security engineer can reduce their mathematical re-derivation work drastically for the covered patterns.



Use of Funds


This grant funds the transition of Symproof from a specialized internal tool to a public-grade security standard.

Each tier of funding unlocks a more complex "Domain Library," expanding the safety net for Ethereum developers and auditors.


Tier 1: Open Source Foundation (<$25k)

The case study documents that boundary explicitly.

We propose to improve its usability and reliability by addressing the currently known drawbacks that prevent FlashSyn from wider adoption, extend it into a continuous monitoring system for EVM-compatible chains, and release the result as an open-source tool for the ecosystem.


Motivation


Modern DeFi exploits are increasingly compositional: attackers construct multi-step strategies that span multiple protocols and exploit assumptions that only break under composition.


A canonical attack pipeline looks as follows:

  1. An attacker enters with capital, potentially obtained via a flash loan
  2. Manipulate price or liquidity in one protocol
  3. Exploit mispriced collateral or accounting in another
  4. Extract back the capital, possibly repay the flash loan, and extract profit


Each step is valid in isolation; the protocols operate as they are intended to, but the systemic vulnerability emerges only when actions are composed.


This shift is well documented and relevant for Ethereum in 2026:

  • Industry data confirms the trend: flash loan and manipulation attacks account for a large share of DeFi losses, often involving multiple protocols: https://www.halborn.com/reports/top-100-defi-hacks-2025
  • Ethereum alone saw 92 incidents and ~$470M in losses in H1 2025, many tied to pricing and logic flaws in composable systems: https://thedefiant.io/news/research-and-opinion/ethereum-hit-by-most-security-incidents-in-h1-2025-slowmist
  • FlashSyn models attacks explicitly as "sequences of actions across DeFi protocols" : https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.10708

Moat is an open-source, decentralized pre-execution transaction-level firewall for smart contracts.


It is for any protocol team that wants to shrink their attack surface — especially teams shipping fast, teams too early-stage to afford the audit they should have before going to production, and teams trying to convince risk-averse LPs that their funds are safe.

Moat originated as an internal solution in response to that exact pressure: running a DeFi protocol where security was the core promise and needing a practical way to back it up.


The Solution

It sits in front of your critical functions — deposits, withdrawals, swaps, anything you choose — and emulates every incoming transaction before it touches your protocol.
By then, funds are often already gone.

Neither is a permissively-licensed primitive a lean team can drop in and run with its own simple rules.


Lean DeFi teams in 2026 — increasingly shipping with LLM-assisted audits and no firewall budget — are exactly the buyer with nothing to drop in today.

Moat persists underneath as the place where the protocol-specific, non-outsourceable rules live: the invariants only the team can write.

Milestone 1 — ~10 ETH

On-chain modifier and force-through state machine, self-hosted off-chain validator with the rule runtime for both Foundry-style invariants and Brevis-proven statistical rules, basic rule template set.

Implementation is well advanced — the grant covers the final stretch and security review before public release.

$300M+ lost to DeFi exploits in 2025 (DeFiLlama).

Any team with M1 deployed is no longer a soft target.


Milestone 2 — ~8 ETH

Decentralized AVS on EigenLayer / Symbiotic.

Data-feed integrations (ChainSecurity, Chainlink, third-party threat intel), richer rule templates.

Removes the last trusted third party, which makes the firewall credible to LPs.


Milestone 3 — ~4 ETH

Preset rule library covering the most common exploits across lending, AMM, vaults, and staking.
Moat is the floor — something you can have from day one, before you have the budget or the team for anything else.

accountable.title: EVMcrispr
snippets:
EVMcrispr is an open-source toolkit for composing, simulating, and executing complex blockchain transactions safely.


Write human-readable scripts that batch multiple operations into single transactions, simulate them on chain forks, and verify outcomes with assertions, all before touching real funds.


What you can do with EVMcrispr:

  • Simulate before you execute. Fork any EVM chain (Ethereum, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, Polygon, Gnosis, and more), run your transactions in a sandbox, manipulate state, and assert expected outcomes.
  • Batch complex operations. Combine token approvals, swaps, governance votes, treasury movements, and contract deployments into single atomic transactions.
  • Interact with any smart contract. Call any function on any contract with automatic ABI resolution, proxy detection, and type checking.
  • Manage DAOs. Full Aragon DAO support: install apps, manage permissions, create tokens, and execute governance proposals.
  • Work with on-chain and off-chain data. Read contract state, resolve ENS names, fetch HTTP APIs, parse JSON, and use the results in your scripts.
  • Automate with logic. Variables, conditionals (if/else), loops (for, while), user-defined functions, array operations, and string manipulation.
  • Integrate with AI. An MCP server and CLI enable AI agents to compose and execute blockchain transactions.


Proven in production: EVMcrispr has been adopted by a wide range of DAOs and decentralized organizations to handle governance, treasury operations, and protocol upgrades.

Projects like Curve, Aragon, NFTX, 1Hive, Giveth, TECommons, BrightID, Agave, and DAppNode have relied on it to compose and execute complex on-chain votes, batching permission changes, token mints, funding allocations, contract upgrades, and even DAO chain migrations, into single, auditable transactions.

For many of these communities, EVMcrispr became the standard way to safely prepare and simulate important proposals before they go to a vote, reducing the risk of costly mistakes in high-stakes DAO operations.


Real-world impact: EVMcrispr was used to simulate and encode the transaction that activated TheDAO Security Fund, a single batched call that safely moved over $220M in ETH and DAO tokens to establish Ethereum's largest security initiative.


EVMcrispr is free, open source (AGPL-3.0), and available at evmcrispr.com.


What we'll do with the funding:

  • Under $5k: Cover ongoing maintenance, hosting, and infrastructure costs.

Continue bug fixes and community support.
  • $5k–$10k: Fund development of new security-focused features: expanded simulation assertions and improved error reporting for safer transaction composition.

Cover travel costs for in-person workshops (such as Barcelona and Cannes, March 2026).
  • $10k–$25k: All of the above, plus develop a comprehensive educational program: written tutorials, video walkthroughs, and workshop curriculum for teaching blockchain operations security using EVMcrispr.

Expand simulation backend capabilities (such as cross-chain simulations).
  • $25k–$50k: All of the above, plus expand MCP capabilities with built-in security guidelines that leverage existing assertion mechanisms to enforce safer transaction composition.

Expand the workshop program to multiple events.
  • $50k+: All of the above, plus launch a community solutions forum, a curated, searchable knowledge base where users can share and discover proven approaches to common blockchain operations challenges.
